findings.title: Withdrawal answers an earlier refusal
findings.claim: The focus command to turn away meets a wider pattern in which people turn from signs and the messenger is told to turn away from one who has turned from the reminder; withdrawal therefore reads as a response to refusal, with agency and cause distinct.
findings.mechanism: The focus imperative أَعْرِضْ carries the ordinary act of withdrawing attention from the addressed group. In 15:81, signs are given and the people turn away from them; in 53:29, the supplied surface commands turning away from one who has turned from the reminder. Their contact makes the focus withdrawal a relational answer to refusal rather than an unexplained social cutoff.
findings.reader_payoff: The turn-away command becomes newly legible as a boundary after rejected guidance: the messenger is released from pressing the same argument, while the group's refusal and his response remain distinct.
findings.containment: These are wider parallels, not an assertion that 32:30 shares their audience or full setting. The focus names only the group addressed, and the parallels do not establish that the command forbids every later word or act.

epistemic.reason: The cross-run support is trusted and the exact supplied Arabic in 15:81 and 53:29 gives concrete relation-level triggers; target morphology is not projected, so the comparison remains bounded.

findings.title: Withdrawal with the horizon still open
findings.claim: The focus pairs turning away with waiting, so disengagement can suspend the immediate exchange while keeping attention on an outcome; wider examples of bounded withdrawal and reciprocal waiting make the pause, rather than indifference, newly visible.
findings.mechanism: أَعْرِضْ carries withdrawal from the group and ٱنتَظِرْ keeps the addressee oriented toward a future event. The command in 6:68 bounds withdrawal from a disputatious setting until the discourse changes, while 11:122 pairs a command to wait with the other side's waiting. These independent relations meet the focus's two coordinated imperatives and frame withdrawal as a pause with an open horizon.
findings.reader_payoff: The reader can see the turn-away and wait commands working together: the immediate exchange recedes while attention remains on what will come.
findings.containment: The wider parallels illustrate bounded disengagement and mutual waiting; they do not set the precise duration of 32:30 or identify the awaited object. The focus's ordinary commands remain intact.

epistemic.reason: The originating walk is legacy-unbound, while exact target Arabic and connection notes support the two bounded comparisons; no 32:29 timetable is asserted.

findings.title: One waiting interval, unequal forecasts
findings.claim: The paired focus forms place both sides in a shared future-facing interval; 9:52 shows that reciprocal waiting can hold opposed forecasts, while 10:20 places the unseen timetable with God. Their matching posture therefore does not establish equal expectations, control of timing, or outcomes.
findings.mechanism: ٱنتَظِرْ is an imperative to wait and مُّنتَظِرُونَ names the group as waiting, so both sides are held in one waiting frame. In 9:52, each side waits for a different outcome from the other; 10:20 assigns the unseen timetable to God rather than either party. These independent triggers meet the focus's matched forms and distinguish shared waiting from equal forecasts or control.
findings.reader_payoff: The reader can feel the shared suspense while leaving the sides' expectations and eventual results distinct.
findings.containment: The parallels demonstrate that reciprocal waiting can accompany opposed forecasts and a timetable outside either party's control; they do not assign exact confidence, taunting, or outcomes to the group in 32:30. The group may share only the interval, and the focus leaves its awaited object unstated.

epistemic.reason: The trusted publication is supported by exact focus forms and the supplied 9:52 and 10:20 surfaces; unbound HFT alternatives remain possibilities about posture, not adjudicated motives.
